clue.text: Hear about stiff exam after university game

indicators.note: the word for hear goes round the other pieces, as if about them

parts.note: to catch a remark is to hear it

indicators.note: the exam abbreviation is placed after the university letter

parts.note: a stiff is a corpse, so its examination is a post-mortem, abbreviated PM

explanation.surface: A student hears about an autopsy following time at university, then talks about a match.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'stiff' is slang for a corpse, so its exam is the post-mortem; 'game' is the definition, a knockout fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: A knockout fixture in a trophy competition is a kind of game.

indicators.note: to want is to lack, so the broadcaster's nickname loses its first letter

parts.note: Auntie is the affectionate British nickname for the BBC

explanation.surface: A liberated broadcaster is looking for someone to run it.
explanation.walkthrough: AUNTIE, the BBC's nickname, lacks its leader A.
explanation.definitionFit: To free something tied is to loosen its knots; the verb is a synonym.

clue.text: No-fly zone confines artist touring very big desert

indicators.note: the zone holds things inside, and here the painter's name holds the other pieces
the painter's name goes round the size letters and the word for desert, as if touring them

parts.note: Claude Monet, the French Impressionist painter
OS is the clothing-size abbreviation for outsize
to desert a post is to quit it

explanation.surface: A restricted zone keeps a painter in while he tours a vast desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confines' reinforces the container: the painter's name holds the rest. The definition is a joke: a net that keeps flies out, a zone where none may fly.
explanation.definitionFit: Mesh hung over a bed keeps biting insects away, a playful zone where no flies are allowed.

clue.text: Energy target put back for lab equipment

indicators.note: the pieces are read in the reverse direction, put back to front

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
a butt is a target, as at an archery range
to put something down is to set it

explanation.surface: An energy target is postponed in favour of buying laboratory kit.
explanation.walkthrough: E, BUTT and SET read in order spell EBUTTSET; 'back' reverses the whole string.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass cylinder closed at one end is standard chemistry laboratory apparatus.

clue.text: Kremlin made cash changing its old symbols

indicators.note: the letters of the three words change places to make a new phrase

explanation.surface: The Kremlin earned money by abandoning its old Soviet emblems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its' refers back to the Kremlin, so the definition is the Soviet emblems.
explanation.definitionFit: The crossed tools on the Soviet flag were the emblem of the USSR, the Kremlin's former regime.

indicators.note: the cow-noise and temperature letter sit inside the call for quiet

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: A cold, still flat sits under a low temperature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' is the cattle verb, not 'not high'.
explanation.definitionFit: A level, even surface with no bumps is flat; the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Lure foreign noble into bishop's office

indicators.note: the French title is placed inside the bishop's seat

parts.note: a see is a bishop's seat or diocese
duc is French for duke

explanation.surface: A bishop tempts a visiting aristocrat into his study.
explanation.definitionFit: To lure someone is to tempt or entice them; the verbs are synonyms.

indicators.note: in a down answer the hotel letter sits under the pair, holding it up

parts.note: in cricket a pair is two ducks, two noughts, written as two Os
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A couple admire a hotel: how nice it is.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'pair' in cricket is a batter out for nought in both innings, hence OO.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of pleasure or admiration, much like saying 'how lovely'.

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
nana is British slang for a fool

explanation.surface: A boss tells a clown to take charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is the metal, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for the most important person in a group, the boss.

definitions.meaning: the Stasi was the East German secret police; with 's added it reads as one word
a state of standstill or inertia

explanation.surface: The secret police are criticised for doing nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A state of standstill or inactivity, where nothing moves or changes, and the East German force's name plus 's.

clue.text: Members eat one dish prepared centrally in vessel

indicators.note: the members take the other letters inside them, as if eating

parts.note: MPs are Members of Parliament
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the dish is prepared, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Parliamentarians eat a meal cooked in the middle of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' looks like body parts but means MPs. 'Prepared' rearranges DISH as DSHI. The definition is an adverb of place on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A nautical adverb meaning amidships, halfway along a ship's length.

indicators.note: only the opening four letters of the violinist's name are kept

parts.note: Yehudi Menuhin was a celebrated violinist

explanation.surface: A star violinist's best four lessons to choose from.
explanation.walkthrough: MENUHIN keeps only its top four letters, dropping HIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A list of dishes to pick from for each course of a meal.

indicators.note: the letters are led astray into a different order

explanation.surface: A detective's traditional coat fools a technocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' is slang for a private detective.
explanation.definitionFit: The belted raincoat is the stereotypical outfit of the hard-boiled private eye.

clue.text: Intercept bad ball, ignoring wings, moving to middle

indicators.note: the letters of the first word are rearranged, made bad
the outer letters of the word are dropped, leaving its centre

explanation.surface: A fielder intercepts a poor ball while drifting in from the wings.
explanation.walkthrough: INTERCEPT rearranged gives CENTRIPET; 'ball' without its wings is AL.
explanation.definitionFit: A physics term for a force directed towards the centre of a circular path.

parts.note: vert is green in heraldry
E is the physics symbol for energy
a bra is an undergarment that supports

explanation.surface: Someone backs a cause and also supports green energy.
explanation.definitionFit: Each bone of the spine holds up the back, so it supports it.

clue.text: Eastern US city unconvincing in battle

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
a lame excuse is an unconvincing one

explanation.surface: An American city in the east puts up a weak showing in a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1942 North African desert clash in the Second World War.

indicators.note: turned round, as in a revolution, the remaining letters read backwards
letters are scooped out of the middle of the weapon

explanation.surface: The old sailor of the poem carries a radical, gutted whaling weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hollowed-out' removes RPO from the inside of HARPOON, leaving HAON; 'revolutionary' reverses it. Coleridge's poem is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: The ark's builder is the Bible's oldest seafarer, a witty twist on Coleridge's poem title.

clue.text: Let's withdraw oar from corrupt car-boot sale

indicators.note: the letters of the sale are corrupted into a new order once the boat paddle is withdrawn

parts.note: taken as written; its letters are removed from the pool

explanation.surface: Someone pulls a rowing oar out of a dodgy car-boot sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdraw ... from' takes O, A, R out of CARBOOTSALE; the remaining letters are rearranged. A car-boot sale is a British flea market held from car boots.
explanation.definitionFit: A let is a hindrance, as in the legal phrase 'without let or hindrance'.

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man

explanation.surface: A father is wearing women's clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiresome bore or nuisance is a drag, colloquially also called a pain.

clue.text: Mr Bean jogged behind docked dog — this one?

definitions.text: Mr Bean jogged behind docked dog — this one?

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come behind the shortened word
a docked tail is cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as a word, then trimmed

indicators.note: the comedian's name is jogged into a different order

explanation.surface: A comedy character runs behind a dog with a cropped tail and asks what breed it is.
explanation.walkthrough: DOG docked is DO; 'jogged' rearranges MR BEAN as BERMAN. The breed traditionally has a docked tail.
explanation.definitionFit: The German guard-dog breed is famous for its cropped tail, fitting the docked dog of the clue.

indicators.note: the letters are tipsy and stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A drinker insists he is sober.
explanation.definitionFit: Said as an exclamation, it is an oath of truthfulness like 'truly' or 'I promise'.

clue.text: Ring put in box? It's stuffed in drawer

indicators.note: the ring shape is placed inside the box

parts.note: a carton is a cardboard box
O is ring-shaped

indicators.note: stuffed as in beaten up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone puts a ring in a box, which is then crammed into a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffed' rearranges ITS as IST. 'Drawer' means a person who draws, not furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who draws comic strips or caricatures is a kind of illustrator.

definitions.meaning: a harbour town on the Isle of Man
to hull fruit is to strip off its outer skin

explanation.surface: A list of harbours: one on the Isle of Man, then Hull.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is also an English port, a decoy; here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The town is a harbour on the Isle of Man's west coast, and to strip skin from fruit is a synonym of hull.

clue.text: That lot close to the top show spirit

indicators.note: the closing letter is brought up to the top of this down entry

parts.note: those means that group, that lot

explanation.surface: A group near the summit shows team spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: THOSE has its last letter moved to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The characteristic spirit or guiding beliefs of a group or culture.

indicators.note: a confused person is bamboozled, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A smooth doctorate-holder confuses an assistant.
explanation.definitionFit: A service point where users get assistance with problems, typically technical.

indicators.note: the word for verse is missing the effort word

parts.note: poetry is verse
a try is an attempt or effort

explanation.surface: He wrote poems without trying hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Allan, the American writer of tales and poems such as The Raven.

clue.text: Memorable start in Cowes — yacht founders

indicators.note: the opening letter of the town name is taken
a ship that founders sinks, so the letters are wrecked

explanation.surface: A memorable opening to Cowes regatta: a yacht sinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowes is a sailing town on the Isle of Wight.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchy tune is easily remembered, so the adjectives are close synonyms.

indicators.note: to cook the books is to fiddle them, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An introduction: cook, R. Stein, the celebrity chef.
explanation.walkthrough: Rick Stein is a well-known British TV chef.
explanation.definitionFit: To introduce something into a slot or text is to put it in; synonyms.

parts.note: to eye someone up is to ogle them
lass is a word for a girl

explanation.surface: A man ogles a German girl through his monocle.
explanation.definitionFit: A monocle is a single lens worn to aid sight, the classic prop of a leering gent.
